title: From left Seeley's Electric, Capitol Theatre, dress shop, and post office
description: Hartland’s theatre history dates back to 1914, when silent movies were shown at the Lyric Theatre in Forester Hall (Lower Main, building beside United Church). By 1918, the Starr Theatre operated in the same hall, continuing the tradition of silent films, now accompanied by pianists. In 1922, the Neighborhood Theatre opened for the winter in Burtts Hall on upper Main Street, offering audiences fine talking pictures. After a fire, Wendel Tedlie sold the partially burned building to a group from Saint John, who remodelled and reopened it as the Capitol Theatre. During the war, the government presented films supporting the war effort, including footage of the Carleton York Regiment receiving its colours from His Majesty the King, a ceremony in which Lt. J. Arthur Thornton, son of Mrs. Dwight Ebbett, accepted them. In November 1947, plans were announced for a new, modern Capitol Theatre to be constructed south of the Post Office (now the library), at a cost of $100,000 and managed by Hugh Best, followed by Frank McMullin and John Gillin. The accompanying photo shows the new theatre, which opened on May 21, 1948, with its first movie: “The Fabulous Texan.” Glen Cummings purchased and remodelled it in 1969. The theatre building was torn down in 1986.
